Chapter 19

Assembling a trace from spans that arrive in any order

Four things that are true of real trace data, each of which breaks the obvious implementation — and the four fixes, each a few lines.

By the end of this chapter

Turn a flat list of spans into one tree that always renders, and say out loud what was missing.

Read the four numbered points, because each is a different failure of groupBy(parentId) and each is common enough to hit within a day of real data.

Index first, link second

Indexing every span by id before linking anything is what makes arrival order irrelevant. The version that links as it walks works perfectly on data sorted by start time and drops children on data that is not — and the database returns rows in arrival order, which is neither.

A span whose parent is absent is not dropped. It becomes a root and is counted, because the service that would have sent the parent is very often the one that failed.

Cycles, and why they are worth checking for

A cycle in a span tree is always a data bug — a malformed sender, a replayed span with a rewritten id. The cost of not checking is not a wrong picture: it is a stack overflow during render, which takes the tab with it. Twenty lines to turn a crash into a note in the interface.

Self time, which is the number people want

A span that took 900ms is not interesting if 890ms of it was one child. A span that took 900ms with 40ms of children is 860ms of unexplained work in *that* service — which is where the problem is. The clamp at zero matters too: children can legitimately sum to more than the parent when they ran concurrently, and a negative "self time" is a number nobody can interpret.

Flatten iteratively, and reverse the push

Recursion here would be simpler and would blow the stack on exactly the traces that most need looking at — a service retrying in a loop produces a chain thousands deep, and *that* trace is the bug report.

The reversed push is a one-line detail with a visible symptom: without it, each level’s children render backwards, and the waterfall looks like the request happened in the wrong order.

And then say what was missing

orphanCount and hadCycle are on the returned trace so that the interface can say "3 spans have no parent in this trace" rather than rendering a plausible tree in silence. A missing gateway span is frequently the answer, and a viewer that hides it is a viewer that costs somebody an hour.

Checkpoint

  • Spans shuffled into a random order assemble into the same tree.
  • A trace with no root renders as one tree under a synthetic one, and says so.
  • A trace with a cycle renders rather than crashing.
